questions.question: PPO's headline benefit over plain actor-critic is what?
options: It removes the critic, so there is one network instead of two
It bounds the reward so the advantage never explodes
It lets you take many gradient epochs on one rollout without the policy running away from the data
It replaces the discount factor with an explicit trust region on the discounted return, bounding each update's effect
questions.explanation: Rollouts are the expensive part. The clipped surrogate keeps multi-epoch reuse safe by removing the incentive to move any sample's probability more than ε away from the policy that collected it.

questions.question: A sample has A_t < 0. On which side of the corridor does the clip switch off its gradient?
options: When the ratio rises above 1 + ε
When the ratio falls below 1 − ε
Only when the ratio equals exactly 1
Never — clipping only engages for positive advantages
questions.explanation: For a bad action the update pushes its probability down, so the ratio moves downward; the floor at 1 − ε is what stops it. The two clip boundaries are direction-matched to the sign of the advantage.

questions.question: Once a sample lands outside its clip boundary, what does it contribute to the policy gradient on that step?
options: The same magnitude with the sign flipped, pulling the ratio back
The full gradient scaled down by ε
Exactly zero — the objective is flat there, so the sample stops moving θ
Only the value-loss part survives; the policy-gradient part is halved rather than removed
questions.explanation: clip() makes the surrogate a constant in that region, and the derivative of a constant is zero. The sample is not reversed or damped; it simply stops contributing until the ratio drifts back inside.

questions.question: Why is the ratio always computed as exp(log π_θ − log π_old) rather than as π_θ / π_old?
options: Because the log-space form is numerically stable when both probabilities are tiny, where the direct quotient underflows
Because exp() is cheaper than division on a GPU
Because the quotient form would need a separate gradient rule
Because the log form keeps the ratio bounded inside [1-eps, 1+eps], which the raw quotient is not
questions.explanation: Token- or long-horizon probabilities are routinely 1e-30 or smaller; dividing two such numbers loses most of the mantissa or hits zero. Subtracting logs keeps full precision, and the ratio itself is unbounded either way.

questions.question: Sixty updates in, your clip fraction sits at 0.002 and mean KL is essentially zero, while return improves painfully slowly. What does that diagnose?
options: The policy is drifting too far each update — lower the learning rate and cut K epochs until mean KL settles
Advantage normalization is broken — the advantages must be near-constant
ε is too small — widen the corridor from 0.2 to 0.3 so the clip has room to engage again
The updates are too timid — the corridor is never reached, so raise LR or K epochs
questions.explanation: A clip fraction near zero means the constraint is never binding, so it is not what limits you; the healthy band is roughly 0.1–0.3. Widening ε would loosen a constraint that is already inactive.

questions.question: How does PPO relate to TRPO, its predecessor?
options: PPO keeps TRPO's hard KL constraint on every update and solves it with conjugate gradients, which is why it needs no clipping term
PPO trades TRPO's hard trust region for a first-order clipped surrogate — no constrained solve, similar behavior in practice
PPO abandons the trust-region idea entirely and relies on global gradient-norm clipping to keep updates small
PPO is TRPO with the critic removed and the mean reward over a group of sampled completions used as the baseline
questions.explanation: TRPO's guarantee came from an explicit KL constraint that needs a conjugate-gradient solve every update; PPO approximates the same 'stay near π_old' intent with one clipping line and plain SGD. Removing the critic for a group baseline is GRPO, not PPO.
